lessons.title: Elizabeth's accession in 1558: a difficult inheritance

before.content_html:
A Throne Worth Worrying About

When Elizabeth I became queen on 17 November 1558, she inherited a kingdom of about three million people, a half-empty treasury and a Church torn between Catholic and Protestant. England was a small country on the edge of Europe, dwarfed by the empire of King Philip II of Spain and locked in fear of Calais’s recent loss to France. Elizabeth was twenty-five, unmarried and untested. Her advisors, led by William Cecil, expected immediate trouble.

Key Fact

Elizabeth inherited four overlapping problems in 1558: questions about her legitimacy and gender, a Crown debt of around £300,000, deep religious division, and a hostile France with troops in Scotland.

Society and Government

Elizabethan society was a strict hierarchy. At the top sat the monarch, then nobles (about 50 great families), then the gentry, yeomen, tenant farmers, labourers and the homeless poor. About ninety per cent of people lived in the countryside. Government ran from the Crown outwards: the queen made decisions with the Privy Council, Parliament granted taxes and passed statutes, and Lord Lieutenants and Justices of the Peace ran the counties. Without a standing army or police force, Elizabeth’s authority depended on local gentry doing what she said.

The Virgin Queen: Legitimacy and Gender

Elizabeth’s position was legally fragile. Her mother, Anne Boleyn, had been executed in 1536 and Elizabeth had been declared illegitimate by Parliament. To Catholics across Europe, that ruling still stood — making Mary, Queen of Scots, a granddaughter of Henry VII through a legitimate Tudor line, the rightful queen of England. Pope Paul IV refused to recognise Elizabeth at her accession.

Gender added another problem. Many believed a woman could not rule alone. The Scottish Protestant John Knox had published The First Blast of the Trumpet Against the Monstrous Regiment of Women in 1558, attacking female rulers as unnatural. Marriage was the obvious solution because it would produce an heir and add a male partner, but every choice carried danger: a foreign Catholic prince could make England a satellite of Spain or France; an English noble would unbalance the court.

Students often imagine Elizabeth confidently rejected marriage from the start. In 1558–59, the opposite was true: Parliament petitioned her to marry within months of her accession, she entertained serious negotiations with Philip II of Spain and Archduke Charles of Austria, and the ‘Virgin Queen’ image was largely cultivated later. The early years were a real crisis of choice, not a grand strategy.

Her Character and Strengths

Despite her difficult position, Elizabeth had significant assets. She had been carefully educated by Roger Ascham, was fluent in Latin, French, Italian and some Greek, and could quote Scripture from memory. She had survived years of suspicion under her half-sister Mary I, including imprisonment in the Tower in 1554, and emerged politically cautious. She was also charismatic in public — her London entry in January 1559 was a deliberate display of accessibility, with Elizabeth stopping the procession to receive a Bible from a child actor representing Truth.

Key Fact

Elizabeth’s personal strengths — education, political caution learnt under Mary I, and skill at public display — partially offset her weak legal position. Her January 1559 London entry was carefully staged Protestant theatre.

Financial Weakness

The treasury Elizabeth inherited was effectively bankrupt. The Crown owed about £300,000, much of it borrowed at high interest from Antwerp bankers. Mary I had spent heavily on the war against France that ended with the loss of Calais. The coinage had been debased by Henry VIII and Edward VI to pay for earlier wars, meaning the silver content of coins had been deliberately reduced — this caused inflation and damaged trust in English money. Without sound finances, Elizabeth could not afford a war, even if one was forced on her.

Religious Divisions

England had changed religion four times in twenty-five years: Catholic under Henry VIII, more Catholic in detail; Protestant under Edward VI from 1547; firmly Catholic again under Mary I from 1553, with about 280 Protestants burnt as heretics; and now Elizabeth, raised Protestant, on the throne. Many of England’s most experienced bishops were Marian Catholics. Returning Protestant exiles, who had fled to Geneva or Frankfurt under Mary, brought back radical ideas. Elizabeth needed a settlement that would not trigger civil war — the lesson of France in the 1560s loomed large.

The French Threat

The most immediate danger in 1558 was France. King Henry II of France was hostile, allied to Scotland through the ‘Auld Alliance’, and his daughter-in-law was Mary, Queen of Scots — who was already publicly quartering the arms of England on her royal display, advertising her claim. French troops were stationed in Scotland under Mary of Guise, the regent for her daughter. England’s northern border was therefore exposed to a Catholic, French-backed kingdom that contained Elizabeth’s strongest rival.

Calais had been English since 1347. Its loss to France in January 1558 — ten months before Elizabeth’s accession — was a humiliation associated with Mary I, who reportedly said the word would be found written on her heart. For Elizabeth in 1558, Calais was not just a lost port; it was proof that France could push England back, that English military power was overstretched, and that the war Mary I had joined for Philip II had cost England real territory for nothing.

An Inheritance Worth Dreading

By December 1558, Elizabeth’s government was already drafting a religious settlement, opening peace talks with France at Cateau-Cambrésis, and recalling exiles. The young queen’s strengths were real but limited: she could not change her gender, her debts or her enemies overnight. The first months of the reign were not a triumphant Tudor moment — they were crisis management with Cecil at her elbow.

lessons.title: The 1559 religious settlement and the Church of England

before.content_html:
A Religious Compromise

Within six months of her accession, Elizabeth steered through Parliament the laws known as the religious settlement. The aim was a single national Church that most English people could live with: clearly Protestant in doctrine but recognisably traditional in appearance. William Cecil drove the legislation, Elizabeth oversaw the wording, and Matthew Parker was selected as Archbishop of Canterbury to lead it. The result was a careful compromise — sometimes called the ‘via media’ or middle way.

Key Fact

The 1559 settlement consisted of two Acts: the Act of Supremacy made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church, and the Act of Uniformity imposed a single Book of Common Prayer and standard form of worship across England.

The Act of Supremacy (1559)

The Act of Supremacy reversed Mary I’s reunion with Rome and made Elizabeth Supreme Governor of the Church of England. Henry VIII had used the title ‘Supreme Head’ in 1534, but ‘Governor’ was deliberately softer. It avoided suggesting that a woman was directly head of the Church (which Catholics and conservatives believed only a man could be) and it allowed moderate Catholics to accept the queen’s authority over Church administration without conceding that she was a substitute for the Pope. All clergy, judges and royal officials had to swear an oath of loyalty; refusal meant losing their position.

The Act of Uniformity (1559)

The Act of Uniformity prescribed how everyone in England would worship. It restored a revised version of the 1552 Protestant Book of Common Prayer, with two important changes designed to keep Catholics inside the Church: the wording at communion combined the 1549 (more Catholic) and 1552 (more Protestant) phrasings, so the priest’s words could be read either as Christ being truly present in the bread or as a memorial. Vestments — ornate clerical robes — were retained, in line with what the church had used in 1548. Attendance at the Sunday service was compulsory; failing to attend without good reason meant a fine of 12 pence per week, given to the poor.

When the priest gave bread at communion, he said: “The body of our Lord Jesus Christ… preserve thy body and soul unto everlasting life. Take and eat this in remembrance that Christ died for thee, and feed on him in thy heart by faith with thanksgiving.” The first half (from 1549) suggested the bread really was Christ’s body — a Catholic reading. The second half (from 1552) said remember and do this in your heart by faith — a Protestant reading. A worshipper could choose which half to focus on. This was deliberate: it kept moderate Catholics in church.

The Royal Injunctions

In summer 1559, the Royal Injunctions added 57 detailed rules for clergy and parishes. Bibles in English had to be available in every church; clergy could marry but only with their bishop’s permission; pilgrimages and the use of relics were to stop. Each parish was to keep a register of births, marriages and deaths. Visitations were sent across the country to enforce the new rules and root out Catholic objects: an estimated 400 clergy refused to comply and lost their livings. The visitations also confirmed that Elizabeth’s government would not push compromise so far as to accept obvious Catholic ritual.

Key Fact

The settlement looked Catholic in appearance — vestments, traditional church furnishings, ambiguous communion wording — but Protestant in doctrine: an English Bible, the queen as Supreme Governor, no Pope, and no Mass in Latin.

The Church of England in Society

For most ordinary people, the Church was the most important institution in their daily life. The local parish church baptised children, married couples, buried the dead and ran weekly services that people were legally required to attend. Sunday sermons taught religious doctrine and obedience to the queen — a useful political tool. Bishops sat in the House of Lords. Tithes — a tenth of a person’s annual income or produce — supported clergy, while parish records meant the Church was also the main administrative system for tracking the population.

The settlement also gave the Church a hierarchy: archbishops of Canterbury and York at the top, then 27 bishops, then archdeacons, parish priests and curates. Matthew Parker, a moderate Protestant scholar, was consecrated Archbishop of Canterbury in December 1559 to lead the Church without alarming conservatives.

Initial Impact

Most English people accepted the settlement with little open resistance. About 8,000 parish clergy stayed in post, accepted the new prayer book and adapted. Only around 250 to 400 of these clergy refused, alongside 27 of England’s 30 surviving Marian bishops — the majority of whom had been appointed under Mary I and refused the oath of supremacy. The Pope at first did not encourage open rebellion. Elizabeth herself made it a working principle — in a phrase later attributed to her — not to make windows into men’s souls. Outward conformity was enough; what people privately believed was their own affair, at least for now.

The 1559 settlement is often described as a triumph that ended religious dispute. It was not. Puritans inside the new Church wanted further reform of vestments and prayer book. Catholic recusants wanted the Mass back. The settlement bought peace by being deliberately vague, but every later challenge of the reign — the Northern Rebellion, the papal bull of 1570, the plots around Mary — comes from people who could not accept it. Calling it a ‘solution’ misses thirty years of pressure on a deliberate compromise.

An Uneven Settlement

By the end of 1559, England had a Protestant Church with Catholic dressing, run by a queen who refused to interrogate her subjects’ private beliefs and policed by parish-level fines for missing church. The pragmatic genius of the settlement was that it asked very little of most people in the short term. The cost would come later: the same vagueness that calmed 1559 left the door open for Puritan and Catholic challenges that would shape the rest of the reign.
before.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark Explain Why questions on the 1559 settlement, examiners reward answers that explain the settlement as a deliberate compromise rather than just listing its features. Use specific terminology: via media, Supreme Governor (not Head), Act of Uniformity, Book of Common Prayer, Royal Injunctions, recusancy fine of 12 pence. Examiners’ reports flag candidates who confuse the 1559 settlement with later anti-Catholic legislation — in 1559 the recusancy fine was 12d per week, not the heavy fines of 1581.

The Puritan challenge was real but limited; the Catholic challenge was external as well as internal, with the Pope, Mary, Queen of Scots, and Spain all involved. Use precise dates — 1566 (vestments), 1570 (papal bull), 1571 (Treasons Act), 1581 (recusancy fines raised).

lessons.title: Mary, Queen of Scots arrives in England, 1568–69

before.content_html:
A Cousin in Custody

In May 1568, Mary, Queen of Scots, fled across the Solway Firth in a fishing boat and threw herself on Elizabeth’s mercy. The decision Elizabeth then took — to keep Mary in England rather than restore her in Scotland or send her on to France — created a problem that would last nineteen years and shape every crisis until 1587. Within a year of Mary’s arrival, the north of England was in armed rebellion. To understand why, we have to follow Mary’s story from her birth.

Key Fact

Mary was Elizabeth’s first cousin once removed, granddaughter of Henry VII through his eldest daughter Margaret Tudor. To Catholics, who never accepted Elizabeth’s legitimacy, Mary was the rightful Queen of England.

Mary’s Claim to the English Throne

Mary’s claim was straightforward in Catholic eyes. Henry VII of England had two daughters who survived to adulthood: Mary Tudor (Elizabeth’s grandmother by no line, since Elizabeth descended from Henry VII through his son Henry VIII) and Margaret Tudor, who married James IV of Scotland. Margaret’s grandchild was Mary, Queen of Scots. Born in 1542, Mary became queen of Scotland aged six days old when her father James V died. Because she was the senior surviving Catholic Tudor descendant, Mary held a powerful claim of succession against Elizabeth.

Brought up in France, Mary married the heir to the French throne in 1558 and briefly became queen of France in 1559. While in France, she displayed the arms of England as well as Scotland on her royal banner — a public claim that Elizabeth, declared illegitimate by Parliament after Anne Boleyn’s execution, was a usurper. Mary was a Catholic, by upbringing and by deep conviction. For English Catholics, she was the obvious heir; for Catholic Europe, she was already the rightful queen.

Mary’s Disastrous Years in Scotland

Widowed at eighteen, Mary returned to a Scotland transformed by the Protestant Reformation of 1560. The Scottish Parliament, led by John Knox, had abolished the authority of the Pope and made Catholic Mass illegal. Mary as a personal Catholic monarch in a Protestant country struggled. Her second marriage in 1565 to Lord Darnley, an arrogant English Catholic noble, was a political catastrophe. Within three years, the Scottish nobility had forced her to abdicate and accept her infant son James as king in her place.

In March 1566, Darnley led a group of Scottish lords who burst into the queen’s rooms at Holyroodhouse and stabbed her secretary David Rizzio to death. Mary gave birth to their son James (the future James VI of Scotland and James I of England) in June 1566. In February 1567, Darnley himself was strangled and the house he was staying in blown up. Within three months, Mary married the Earl of Bothwell, the man widely believed to have killed Darnley. Scottish nobles rebelled. Mary was forced to abdicate in July 1567 in favour of her infant son and held prisoner. She escaped in May 1568, lost a battle at Langside near Glasgow, and fled south across the border into England.

Why Elizabeth Could Not Just Send Her Home

When Mary wrote to Elizabeth begging for help, Elizabeth had four options, each with serious problems. Restore Mary by force: this would require an English army marching into Scotland, which would alarm the Protestant Scottish lords now governing the country in the name of Mary’s baby son, and risk an unwanted war. Allow Mary to return to France: this would put a Catholic claimant to the English throne back in France, where her Guise relatives could give her armies and ships. Help Mary go on to Spain: even worse — King Philip II of Spain was already a potential enemy. Keep Mary in England: in some kind of comfortable custody. Elizabeth and Cecil chose this last option, framing it as protective hospitality.

The York and Westminster Conferences, 1568–69

To justify holding Mary, Elizabeth’s government held a quasi-judicial enquiry into the murder of Darnley. It opened at York in October 1568 and continued at Westminster from late November. The Earl of Moray, regent for Mary’s baby son and effectively running Scotland, produced the so-called Casket Letters — documents allegedly proving Mary’s involvement in Darnley’s murder. The conference reached no formal verdict: Elizabeth declared the case ‘not proven’. This non-verdict was politically perfect — it kept Mary tarnished enough to justify continued custody, but innocent enough that her royal status was not openly attacked.

Why Mary in England Was a Crisis

Mary’s presence created a permanent threat for five overlapping reasons.

  • A ready-made Catholic alternative. Any Catholic dissatisfied with Elizabeth now had a queen to rally to without needing a foreign invasion to provide one.
  • Political magnet for the disaffected. Powerful nobles like the Earls of Northumberland and Westmorland could plot in Mary’s name; she became the focus of the 1571 Ridolfi plot, the 1583 Throckmorton plot and the 1586 Babington plot.
  • Foreign support. Spain, France and the Pope all had reasons to back Mary. After Pope Pius V’s 1570 bull excommunicating Elizabeth, supporting Mary became a religious duty for Catholic monarchs.
  • Marriage games. One early proposal was for Mary to marry the Duke of Norfolk, England’s premier Catholic noble. Cecil and Elizabeth saw this for what it was — the construction of a rival Catholic court inside England.
  • Public sympathy. Mary was a fellow anointed queen. Executing her was politically toxic and would alienate Catholic Europe and even some English moderates.
Key Fact

Mary was a permanent threat because she combined a strong Catholic claim, ready-made appeal to disaffected nobles, foreign Catholic backing, marriage potential with English Catholics, and the moral protection of being an anointed queen.

The Norfolk Marriage Plan, 1569

In 1569, several Privy Councillors and nobles backed a plan for Mary to marry Thomas Howard, Duke of Norfolk — the only duke in England, a Protestant on the surface but with Catholic sympathies and immense lands. The plan was supported by some who saw Mary as a future heir; others opposed Cecil’s rising influence and saw a Mary–Norfolk match as a way of restoring traditional noble power. Elizabeth refused the marriage. The Northern Earls, already disillusioned with court politics and now seeing Mary as a potential ally, began the planning that led to the Northern Rebellion of November 1569 — covered in the next lesson.

Students often confuse Mary, Queen of Scots with Mary I of England. They are different people. Mary I was Elizabeth’s Catholic Tudor half-sister, daughter of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon, who reigned 1553–58 and burnt around 280 Protestants as heretics. Mary I died in November 1558 — before this depth study even begins. Mary, Queen of Scots, was Elizabeth’s Catholic Stuart cousin, queen of Scotland from 1542, in England from 1568, executed at Fotheringhay in 1587. The depth study is about the Stuart Mary — not the Tudor one.

A Permanent Problem

By the end of 1569, Elizabeth had a Catholic cousin under house arrest, a north of England in revolt, and a Privy Council divided over what to do next. Mary would never leave England alive. The choice Elizabeth made in May 1568 — to keep her cousin in protective custody — was the one decision around which almost every later threat in this depth study would turn.
before.exam_tip_html: For 16-mark Make and Defend a Judgement questions on Mary’s arrival in England, examiners’ reports note that strong students show the chain of consequences — Mary’s claim, her arrival, the Norfolk plan, the Northern Rebellion. Don’t treat Mary’s arrival as a single event; treat it as a long-running cause that creates the conditions for plots, papal hostility and rebellion. Avoid the common mistake of confusing Mary, Queen of Scots, with Mary I of England — this depth study begins after Mary I has died.

practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct features clearly identified, each developed with precise detail. For example: (1) Mary was descended from Margaret Tudor, eldest daughter of Henry VII, who married James IV of Scotland — making Mary great-granddaughter of Henry VII through a legitimate Tudor line. (2) Mary was Catholic, and to Catholic Europe Elizabeth was illegitimate (Parliament had declared her so after Anne Boleyn’s execution in 1536), so Mary was widely seen as the rightful queen.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Mary, Queen of Scots fled to England in 1568.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained explanation of three reasons. Should include: the murder of David Rizzio in March 1566, by lords led by her husband Darnley, which broke trust between Mary and many of her nobles; Darnley’s own murder in February 1567 and Mary’s subsequent marriage to Bothwell, the prime suspect, which alienated Scottish opinion; her forced abdication in July 1567 and imprisonment; her escape in May 1568, defeat at the Battle of Langside, and lack of alternative refuge close at hand. Reasons should be linked into a clear causal chain.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Elizabeth chose to keep Mary, Queen of Scots in protective custody in England rather than restore her or send her abroad.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation of three or more interconnected reasons. Should cover: the danger of an English army restoring Mary in Scotland alarming the Protestant Scottish lords governing for her infant son; the threat of Mary returning to France, where her Guise relatives could provide armies and ships to support a Catholic claim against Elizabeth; the unacceptable risk of Mary going to Spain and Philip II; the political usefulness of holding Mary in England without verdict, as established by the ‘not proven’ outcome of the York and Westminster conferences; and the sense among Cecil and the Privy Council that custody was the cheapest way to neutralise a permanent threat. Reasons must be linked, not listed.

Secure: Three reasons explained with accurate detail.

Developing: Two reasons explained, or several reasons identified without development.

Emerging: One reason, or general assertions.

For example: (1) Elizabeth refused to meet Mary in person, even after Mary fled to England in May 1568, fearing it would imply formal recognition; she instead held Mary in protective custody at a series of country houses. (2) Elizabeth’s government held the York and Westminster conferences in October 1568 to investigate Darnley’s murder, with the Earl of Moray producing the Casket Letters as evidence; the case was declared ‘not proven’, allowing Mary to be kept in England without formal conviction.

lessons.title: The Revolt of the Northern Earls, 1569–70

before.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark ‘Explain why’ on the Northern Rebellion, examiners want you to explain at least three reasons AND show how they interconnect — lost noble power pushed the Earls into action, Mary’s arrival made action feel worth attempting, and the Norfolk marriage gave them a plausible plan. For the 16-mark judgement, name a specific Privy Council figure (Cecil, Sussex, Walsingham) where the question lets you — the 2023 examiner report flagged vague references to ‘the Council’ as the difference between the top and middle bands. Use period vocabulary: recusancy, Council of the North, excommunication, Privy Council.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Revolt of the Northern Earls, 1569–70.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• It was led by Catholic nobles — specifically the Earls of Northumberland (Thomas Percy) and Westmorland (Charles Neville), with around 4,600 tenants raised in November 1569.
• It included a deliberate religious act — the rebels restored the Catholic Mass at Durham Cathedral on 14 November 1569 and tore up the English Bible and prayer book.
• Its target was Mary, Queen of Scots — the rebels marched south to free her from Tutbury, but Elizabeth had already moved her to Coventry.
• It collapsed without a major battle — the rebels disbanded in December 1569 once the Earl of Sussex raised 14,000 royal troops.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Revolt of the Northern Earls broke out in 1569.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• Loss of noble power — the Earls had been stripped of Crown lands, mining rights and influence on the Council of the North, replaced by ‘new men’ such as William Cecil; rebellion was a way to reclaim status.
• Religious grievance — the 1559 settlement had outlawed the Catholic Mass, and the Earls’ tenants and households remained loyal to Catholicism; restoring the Mass at Durham was central to the rising.
• Mary, Queen of Scots’ arrival in England (May 1568) — placed a Catholic alternative on English soil within reach at Tutbury, making rebellion appear winnable for the first time.
• The Norfolk marriage scheme — the Duke of Norfolk’s plan to marry Mary suggested even southern Protestants might accept her; Norfolk’s arrest in October 1569 forced the Earls to act before they were summoned.

Mastering: Two reasons fully explained with precise period detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification of a cause without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Revolt of the Northern Earls (1569–70) was significant for Elizabeth’s reign.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the 1570 papal bull (Regnans in Excelsis)
• the Council of the North
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three explained reasons (using both stimulus points AND at least one of own knowledge) with clear causal links between them.

Indicative content:
• 1570 papal bull (stimulus) — Pius V’s Regnans in Excelsis excommunicated Elizabeth and absolved Catholics of allegiance, officially linking Catholicism to treason and shaping every later plot.
• Council of the North (stimulus) — reorganised under loyal Protestant control after the revolt, ending the old independent power of the Percy and Neville families and centralising Tudor authority in the north.
• 1571 Treasons Act and harsher recusancy fines — Parliament responded by making it a capital offence to deny Elizabeth’s right to rule and increased pressure on Catholics who refused Anglican services.
• Shift in the form of Catholic resistance — the failure of open rebellion pushed Catholic opposition underground into the Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583) and Babington (1586) plots, requiring Walsingham’s spy network.
• Mary, Queen of Scots became the focus of every later threat — she had been the rebels’ goal, and remained the gravitational centre of plots until her execution in 1587.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections between factors.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description of events without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (Mary’s arrival as main cause):
• Mary fled to England in May 1568; before then the Earls had grievances but had not rebelled. Her presence at Tutbury made the rebellion’s plan possible.
• Without a Catholic figurehead within striking distance, freeing her could not have been the rebels’ immediate aim; she gave the rising its goal.
• Every later plot (Ridolfi, Throckmorton, Babington) also pivoted on Mary — she was the gravitational centre of Catholic resistance from 1568 onwards.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• Loss of noble power (stimulus) — both Earls had been stripped of lands, mines and influence on the Council of the North; rebellion was about reclaiming status, with religion as a unifying banner.
• 1559 religious settlement (stimulus) — making Catholic worship illegal created a decade of grievance among northern tenants and gave the rising its symbolic act at Durham; without religion the Earls could not have raised 4,600 men.
• The Norfolk marriage scheme (own knowledge) — Norfolk’s arrest in October 1569 was the immediate trigger; the Earls had to act before they were summoned. Mary’s presence enabled the plan, but Norfolk’s arrest forced the timing.

Justified judgement: Mary’s arrival was the trigger that turned long-standing grievances into action, but the underlying causes — lost noble power and the 1559 settlement — were the deeper drivers. A strong response weighs Mary as catalyst against these long-term factors and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed, judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors; judgement asserted rather than supported.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Elizabeth’s response to the Revolt of the Northern Earls.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Mass executions across the north — around 450 rebels, mostly poorer tenants chosen by lottery, were hanged so every northern village saw retribution.
• Confiscation of rebel lands — Crown seized estates from the Percy and Neville families, breaking their long-term regional wealth.
• Reorganisation of the Council of the North — placed under loyal Protestant control to end the Earls’ old dominance.
• Pursuit of fugitive leaders — Northumberland was eventually returned by the Scots and beheaded at York in 1572.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Mary, Queen of Scots became central to the threat against Elizabeth after 1568.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• Her dynastic claim — as Henry VII’s great-granddaughter and a Catholic, Mary had a strong claim to the English throne if Elizabeth could be removed; this made her a natural figurehead.
• Her physical presence in England — from May 1568 she was held in English custody (Tutbury, then later Sheffield), within reach of any rising or rescue plot rather than safely abroad.
• The 1570 papal bull — once Pius V had excommunicated Elizabeth, killing or deposing her became a Catholic duty, and Mary was the only credible Catholic replacement.
• The Norfolk marriage scheme of 1569 — suggested even powerful English nobles would back a Mary-led succession, encouraging Catholic plotters to keep trying.

Mastering: Two reasons fully explained with precise period detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without full explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

before.content_html:
After the Northern Earls failed in open battle, Catholic resistance went underground. Between 1571 and 1586 three serious conspiracies aimed to assassinate Elizabeth, free Mary, Queen of Scots, and put her on the English throne with Spanish or French troops behind her. Each one was caught. The reason they were caught matters as much as the plots themselves: Sir Francis Walsingham, Elizabeth’s Principal Secretary, had built the most sophisticated intelligence network in Europe.

Key Fact

The three major plots all centred on Mary, Queen of Scots: the Ridolfi Plot (1571) was a Spanish-backed plan to depose Elizabeth and crown Mary; the Throckmorton Plot (1583) was a French- and Spanish-backed invasion plan; the Babington Plot (1586) aimed to assassinate Elizabeth and was the trap that finally caught Mary.

The Ridolfi Plot, 1571

Roberto Ridolfi was a Florentine banker living in London with contacts in Madrid and Rome. His 1571 plan was to coordinate a Spanish invasion from the Netherlands under the Duke of Alva, an English Catholic rising led by the Duke of Norfolk, and the assassination of Elizabeth — all to put Mary on the throne and marry her to Norfolk.

Walsingham, then ambassador to France, intercepted coded correspondence and worked with Cecil to crack the cipher. Ridolfi himself was abroad when his courier was arrested at Dover with incriminating papers. Norfolk — already pardoned once for his role in 1569 — was arrested, tried for treason and executed in June 1572. Mary remained alive in custody, but Parliament now demanded harsher action against her.

The Throckmorton Plot, 1583

Francis Throckmorton was a young Catholic gentleman who acted as a courier between Mary and the Spanish ambassador in London, Bernardino de Mendoza. The 1583 plan was an invasion by French Catholic forces under the Duke of Guise, funded by Philip II of Spain, accompanied by an English Catholic rising. Walsingham’s agents had been watching Throckmorton for six months.

When his house was searched, agents found a list of English Catholic supporters and details of suitable invasion ports. Under torture, Throckmorton confessed; he was executed in July 1584. Mendoza was expelled from England — the last Spanish ambassador permitted on English soil. Parliament passed the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety, declaring that anyone in whose name a plot was made could be tried and executed. Mary was now legally exposed.

It is easy to picture Mary as the mastermind because every plot was named ‘for Mary’. In reality she was a closely watched prisoner moved between Tutbury, Sheffield, Chartley and Fotheringhay. Ridolfi was the Florentine banker’s scheme; Throckmorton was a courier passing letters; only the Babington Plot produced a letter in Mary’s own hand explicitly approving Elizabeth’s assassination — and even that exists because Walsingham deliberately allowed the correspondence to flow so that she would commit herself in writing. Top-band answers separate Mary’s claim (the magnet) from her active leadership (much smaller than the legend).

Walsingham’s Intelligence Network

By the early 1580s Sir Francis Walsingham — Principal Secretary from 1573 — ran an intelligence service of around 50 agents across England and Europe, paid for partly out of his own pocket. His chief cryptanalyst, Thomas Phelippes, could break almost any contemporary cipher. Agents intercepted letters, opened them, copied them, recoded them and sent them on so the recipients suspected nothing. Catholic priests entering England were tracked from the moment they landed. Imprisoned suspects were interrogated, often under torture authorised by the Privy Council.

For the Mary problem specifically, Walsingham organised what would now be called a sting. He arranged for Mary to be moved to Chartley Hall in 1585 and let her believe she had a secret channel for letters — smuggled in beer barrels by a brewer. Every letter was already being read. The trap was set; he simply needed someone reckless enough to step into it.

The Babington Plot, 1586

Anthony Babington was a wealthy Catholic gentleman in his mid-twenties. In July 1586 he wrote to Mary outlining a plan to assassinate Elizabeth, free Mary, and welcome a Spanish-backed invasion. Walsingham’s team intercepted the letter, read it, copied it — and waited.

Mary’s reply on 17 July 1586 explicitly approved the assassination of Elizabeth. Phelippes added a forged postscript asking Babington to name his fellow conspirators, then resealed the letter and let it through. Babington named them. By August every plotter was in custody. Babington and six others were hanged, drawn and quartered in September 1586. Mary was tried at Fotheringhay Castle in October under the 1585 Act; her own letter sealed her fate.

Key Fact

Mary was tried at Fotheringhay in October 1586 and condemned to death. Elizabeth delayed signing the warrant for months. When she finally signed in February 1587, William Cecil and the Privy Council acted immediately — Mary was beheaded at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587. Elizabeth publicly blamed her secretary, Davison, for sending the warrant.

Why Mary Was Executed in 1587

The execution had multiple causes. The Babington letter gave incontrovertible written proof, removing Elizabeth’s usual legal cover. The 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety had been designed for exactly this. Parliament and the Privy Council, especially William Cecil and Walsingham, had been pushing for years. Spanish preparations for an invasion fleet were already visible — killing Mary removed Catholic Europe’s legitimate alternative monarch and put Spain in a corner. Elizabeth’s own famous prevarication — she signed, then claimed she had not meant the warrant to be used — reflected the political risk: executing an anointed queen was unprecedented and gave Philip II a Catholic martyr to exploit.

Examiners reward answers that connect the plots into a chain rather than describing each in turn. Ridolfi (1571) produced the 1571 Treasons Act and tightened recusancy fines. Throckmorton (1583) produced the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety. Babington (1586) gave the legal proof to use that Act against Mary herself. Each plot drove a tougher law that made the next plot easier to prosecute — and Mary’s execution in 1587 then removed Spain’s legitimate cover, leading directly to the Armada the following year.

The plots show two things. First, that the threat to Elizabeth was genuine and persistent — without Walsingham, Cecil, Phelippes and the network they ran, one of these schemes would probably have succeeded. Second, that Elizabeth was not making these decisions alone. The 2023 Edexcel examiners’ report flagged candidates who treated the Privy Council as a vague entity; the named figures — Cecil at Treasury, Walsingham at intelligence, Phelippes on ciphers — are the difference between a vague answer and a top-band one.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Babington Plot, 1586.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• It involved a plan to assassinate Elizabeth — Anthony Babington, a wealthy young Catholic gentleman, wrote to Mary in July 1586 setting out plans to kill the Queen and welcome a Spanish-backed invasion.
• It was uncovered through intercepted ciphered letters — Walsingham’s chief cryptanalyst Thomas Phelippes deciphered the correspondence and added a forged postscript asking Mary to name fellow plotters.
• It directly implicated Mary, Queen of Scots — her reply on 17 July 1586 explicitly approved Elizabeth’s assassination, providing the written evidence used to convict her.
• It led to mass executions — Babington and six co-conspirators were hanged, drawn and quartered in September 1586; Mary was tried at Fotheringhay in October.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Walsingham’s spy network was effective at catching Catholic plotters.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• Scale and reach — around 50 agents in England and Europe, partly funded by Walsingham himself, allowed continuous surveillance of suspected Catholics, foreign embassies and ports of entry.
• Cipher-breaking — Thomas Phelippes could decipher almost any contemporary code; intercepted letters were copied and resealed so plotters never knew they had been read.
• Use of stings and false channels — the Chartley beer-barrel route was a controlled channel that let Mary believe her letters were secret while every word was being read by the Privy Council.
• Authority and tools — the Privy Council could authorise torture of suspects (e.g. Throckmorton) and Walsingham had direct access to Elizabeth and Cecil, so intelligence translated quickly into arrests.

Mastering: Two reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why Mary, Queen of Scots was executed in 1587.
You may use the following in your answer:
• the Babington Plot
• the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links.

Indicative content:
• Babington Plot (stimulus) — Mary’s letter of 17 July 1586 explicitly approved Elizabeth’s assassination; Walsingham and Phelippes had ensured the correspondence was preserved as written evidence.
• 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety (stimulus) — passed after Throckmorton, this law allowed anyone in whose name a plot was made to be tried and executed; it gave the Privy Council a legal route to Mary they had previously lacked.
• Pressure from the Privy Council (own knowledge) — William Cecil (Burghley), Walsingham and Parliament had pressed for Mary’s execution since 1572; once Babington gave them proof, they pushed Elizabeth to act.
• Foreign threat from Spain (own knowledge) — Philip II was already preparing the Armada; killing Mary removed the legitimate Catholic alternative monarch he could install if his invasion succeeded.
• Pattern of plots since 1571 — Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington showed Mary would remain a magnet for conspiracies as long as she lived; only her death would end the cycle.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (Babington evidence as main reason):
• Mary’s 17 July 1586 letter explicitly approved Elizabeth’s assassination — this was direct written treason in her own hand, which Ridolfi and Throckmorton had never produced.
• Without that proof, Elizabeth would have lacked political cover to execute an anointed queen and royal cousin; previous plots had not led to her death.
• The trial at Fotheringhay in October 1586 used the letter as the central piece of evidence under the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• Walsingham’s spy network (stimulus) — the evidence only existed because Walsingham deliberately ran the Chartley sting and Phelippes deciphered the letters; without the network there would be no Babington case to use.
• Spanish invasion plans (stimulus) — by 1586 Philip II was actively preparing the Armada; killing Mary now removed Catholic Europe’s legitimate alternative ruler before any invasion landed, making her execution a strategic decision as much as a legal one.
• Privy Council pressure (own knowledge) — Cecil and Walsingham had pushed for Mary’s execution since 1572; the Babington letter unlocked years of pent-up political demand, not just the 1586 case.
• 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety (own knowledge) — without that legal framework, the Babington evidence alone would not have made trial of an anointed queen possible.

Justified judgement: The Babington evidence was the immediate trigger, but it only existed because of Walsingham’s sting; only a legal route because of the 1585 Act; and only acted on because of Privy Council pressure and the Spanish threat. A strong response weighs the trigger against these enabling factors and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Use of cipher-breaking — Thomas Phelippes deciphered intercepted letters and even forged postscripts (e.g. asking Babington to name his fellow plotters).
• Network of agents at home and abroad — around 50 spies in England and Europe tracked Catholic priests, courier routes, and foreign embassies including the Spanish ambassador.
• Stings and controlled channels — at Chartley Hall in 1585 Walsingham let Mary believe her letters were being smuggled in beer barrels while every letter was being read.
• Authorised interrogation — suspects such as Francis Throckmorton were arrested and tortured under Privy Council authority until they confessed.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Catholic plots of 1571–87 led to harsher treatment of English Catholics.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• Each plot produced new legislation — the 1571 Treasons Act (after Ridolfi) made denying Elizabeth’s right to rule treason; the 1581 Act increased recusancy fines to £20 a month; the 1585 Act for the Queen’s Surety (after Throckmorton) targeted plotters and their patrons.
• Catholicism became politically associated with foreign invasion — Ridolfi was Spanish-backed, Throckmorton French- and Spanish-backed, Babington again Spanish-backed; the Privy Council framed every English Catholic as a potential fifth column.
• Priests became automatic suspects — the 1585 Act made it treason for a Catholic priest trained abroad to enter England; Walsingham’s network tracked them from arrival.
• The papal bull of 1570 (Regnans in Excelsis) had told Catholics they owed Elizabeth no allegiance, so plots seemed to confirm Catholicism itself was a security threat.

Mastering: Two reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

lessons.title: The road to war with Spain, 1569–87

before.content_html:
In 1558 Philip II of Spain had been Elizabeth’s brother-in-law, briefly proposed marriage, and was the dominant Catholic monarch of Europe. By 1587 his fleet was assembling at Lisbon to invade England. The drift from awkward alliance to open war took thirty years and pulled in religion, money, the Atlantic, and a small group of English seafarers who treated Spanish ships as legitimate prizes. By the mid-1580s a single major incident — English involvement in the Netherlands and Drake’s raid on Cadiz — had made war unavoidable.

Key Fact

Anglo-Spanish relations broke down across four strands: political (Mary’s execution and rival claims to the throne), religious (Protestant England versus Catholic Spain after 1570), commercial (privateering and clashes in the Atlantic), and military (English troops in the Netherlands from 1585 and Drake’s raid on Cadiz in 1587).

Political and Religious Rivalry

Through the 1560s the breakdown was slow. Philip II initially valued England as a buffer against France and tolerated Elizabeth’s Protestantism. The 1570 papal bull Regnans in Excelsis changed the diplomatic weather: Pius V excommunicated Elizabeth and absolved Catholics of allegiance, recasting any Catholic monarch’s duty as removing her. The Ridolfi (1571), Throckmorton (1583) and Babington (1586) plots all featured Spanish backing or Spanish ambassadors. Mary, Queen of Scots was Catholic Europe’s legitimate alternative ruler — her execution in February 1587 removed Philip’s diplomatic restraint.

Religion ran underneath all of this. Philip saw himself as the defender of the Catholic faith; the Counter-Reformation made the survival of Protestant England a personal affront. Recusancy fines, the execution of Catholic priests under the 1585 Act, and English support for the Dutch Protestant rebels all looked, from Madrid, like a Protestant crusade against Catholic Europe.

Commercial Rivalry — Privateering and Drake

Spain claimed a monopoly on trade with its American colonies under the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas. English merchants disagreed. From the 1560s, captains such as John Hawkins (with Crown investment) ran trading voyages into the Spanish Caribbean, and from the early 1570s privateering exploded.

Sir Francis Drake was the most successful and most provocative privateer. In 1572–73 he raided Spanish silver convoys at Nombre de Dios in Panama. Between 1577 and 1580 he circumnavigated the globe in the Golden Hind, plundering Spanish ports along the Pacific coast of South America and returning with around £400,000 of treasure — roughly the value of a year’s Crown revenue. Elizabeth knighted him on his own ship at Deptford in 1581. Philip II read the knighthood as a deliberate insult: the queen of England was endorsing piracy.

Drake is often presented as an unambiguous English hero. The Edexcel B4 spec foregrounds his circumnavigation and his role against the Armada, and you should know those events well. But context matters: Drake had earlier sailed with John Hawkins on Crown-backed voyages that trafficked enslaved Africans to the Spanish Caribbean. The same decades that saw English ‘heroes’ tweak Spanish noses in the Atlantic were also building the early infrastructure of the transatlantic slave trade. Top-band judgement answers can know the spec content without absorbing the ‘Sea Dog’ legend uncritically.

English Involvement in the Netherlands

The Netherlands had been Spanish territory since 1556. Dutch Protestant rebels began the Eighty Years’ War in 1568, and Philip’s response was to send his most ruthless commander, the Duke of Alva, with 10,000 men. Elizabeth had three reasons to worry. A Catholic Spanish-controlled Netherlands sat just across the Channel from Kent. Spanish armies in the Netherlands could ferry to England. And the suppression of Protestantism on her doorstep made her own position weaker.

Through the 1570s Elizabeth offered the Dutch covert support — money, English volunteers, harbour for Dutch ships — without committing troops officially. By 1584–85 the Dutch position was collapsing: William the Silent had been assassinated in July 1584, the Duke of Parma was steadily reconquering Dutch towns, and Antwerp fell in August 1585. In August 1585 Elizabeth signed the Treaty of Nonsuch, agreeing to send 7,400 men under Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, in support of the Dutch.

Leicester’s Expedition, 1585–87

Leicester’s expedition was a strategic and personal embarrassment. He fell out with the Dutch, accepted the title of Governor-General without Elizabeth’s permission (which the queen publicly repudiated), and lost the strategically important towns of Sluys and Deventer — the latter handed to Spain by an English Catholic deserter. His one famous engagement, Zutphen in September 1586, was a small skirmish best remembered for the death of the poet Sir Philip Sidney. Leicester returned home in disgrace in late 1587. The expedition failed militarily but succeeded diplomatically — Philip II treated the Treaty of Nonsuch as a formal declaration of war.

Drake’s Raid on Cadiz, 1587

By the spring of 1587 Philip’s invasion fleet was being assembled at Cadiz, Lisbon and the smaller Iberian ports. Elizabeth authorised Drake to disrupt it. On 19 April 1587 Drake led 23 ships into the harbour of Cadiz, fought past the Spanish defending galleys, and over the next two days destroyed around 30 Spanish warships and supply vessels — including barrels of seasoned wood needed for water casks. He then cruised the Iberian coast for weeks, attacking shipping and the fortress at Sagres.

Drake himself called it ‘singeing the King of Spain’s beard’. The raid did not destroy the Armada — it delayed it by about a year. The destruction of barrel-stave timber proved more important than the ships sunk: when the Armada finally sailed in July 1588, its water and provisions were stored in newer, unseasoned casks that leaked and spoiled at sea.

Key Fact

On 19 April 1587 Drake raided Cadiz with 23 ships, destroying around 30 Spanish vessels and barrels of seasoned wood for water casks. The raid delayed the Spanish Armada by roughly a year and contributed to its supply problems in 1588.

A middle-band answer lists privateering, religion, the Netherlands and Cadiz as separate causes. A top-band answer connects them: the 1570 papal bull (religion) made Catholic plots (Ridolfi, Babington) targeted at Mary politically explosive, which in turn drove Mary’s execution; meanwhile English privateering (Drake) had wrecked the commercial relationship and Crown finances; English troops in the Netherlands from 1585 were the strategic affront; Cadiz in 1587 was the open military challenge. By the time the Armada sailed, all four strands had hardened into a single Spanish decision to invade.

By the end of 1587 every restraining factor was gone. Mary was dead so Philip had a free hand. The Treaty of Nonsuch had committed England to the Dutch revolt. Drake had humiliated Spain at Cadiz. The papal bull was nearly two decades old. The Armada that left Lisbon in May 1588 was the product of all four strands — political, religious, commercial and military — not a sudden Spanish overreaction.
before.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark causation on the road to war, examiners want at least three reasons explained AND interconnected — show how religion (the 1570 bull) drove plots, plots drove Mary’s execution, while privateering and the Netherlands ran in parallel until Cadiz forced the issue. For 16-mark judgement, weigh long-term factors (religion, privateering, the Netherlands) against the short-term trigger (Cadiz 1587 or Mary’s execution) and reach a defended conclusion. Use period vocabulary: privateering, circumnavigation, excommunication, Treaty of Nonsuch, Privy Council.

Indicative content:

• It destroyed Spanish shipping — around 30 warships and supply vessels were destroyed over two days, alongside Drake’s subsequent attacks on Sagres and shipping along the Iberian coast.
• It targeted Spanish supplies, not just ships — the destruction of barrels of seasoned wood for water casks meant the Armada in 1588 had to rely on unseasoned casks that leaked.
• Drake described it himself as ‘singeing the King of Spain’s beard’, signalling its intended humiliation as much as material damage.

• It cost Spain enormous sums — Drake’s circumnavigation alone returned roughly a year of Crown revenue; cumulative privateering losses tied up Spanish convoys and Treasury planning.
• It humiliated Spain on the global stage — raids on silver convoys at Nombre de Dios and ports along the Pacific coast made Philip’s claim to global Catholic primacy look brittle.

• Plots and Mary, Queen of Scots (own knowledge) — Spanish backing for the Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots, and Mary’s execution in February 1587, removed Philip’s diplomatic restraint and gave him a Catholic martyr.
• Cadiz raid (own knowledge) — Drake’s April 1587 attack destroyed around 30 Spanish ships and seasoned timber for casks, delaying the Armada by a year and demanding a military response.

Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (Netherlands as main reason):
• The Treaty of Nonsuch (1585) sent Leicester with 7,400 men to fight Spanish forces; Philip treated it as an open declaration of war.
• A Spanish-controlled Netherlands sat directly across the Channel from Kent — military intervention there was an existential strategic clash, not just a diplomatic dispute.
• Leicester’s loss of Sluys and Deventer (1587) and the parallel Spanish reconquest under Parma kept the conflict active and visible.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• Religious differences (stimulus) — the 1570 papal bull and Counter-Reformation framed Protestant England as a target Philip had a religious duty to overturn; without that framing the Netherlands quarrel might have stayed limited.
• Cadiz raid (stimulus) — April 1587 destroyed around 30 ships and seasoned timber, delayed the Armada by a year and forced Philip into a public response; it was the open military trigger.
• Privateering and Drake (own knowledge) — from the early 1570s English raids on Spanish silver convoys, Drake’s circumnavigation (1577–80) and the 1581 knighthood made the commercial relationship irrecoverable long before 1585.
• Mary’s execution (own knowledge) — February 1587 removed Catholic Europe’s legitimate alternative monarch; Philip’s decision to launch the Armada is hard to read without it.

Justified judgement: The Netherlands intervention was the formal break, but it sat on top of religion (the long-term cause), privateering (the running grievance) and Mary’s execution and Cadiz (the short-term triggers). A strong response weighs Nonsuch as the legal trigger against the deeper religious and commercial causes and reaches a defended overall view.

before.content_html:
In May 1588 the Spanish Armada sailed from Lisbon: 130 ships, around 24,000 sailors and soldiers, under the reluctant command of the Duke of Medina Sidonia. Philip II had ordered the largest amphibious invasion ever attempted in northern Europe. Eight weeks later the surviving fleet was being scattered by storms north of Scotland, and roughly half of it would never reach Spain. Examiners reward students who can explain why — weighing English ships, Spanish supply, leadership, the fireships at Calais and the storms together, not picking one factor.

Key Fact

The Armada failed for four interconnected reasons: English ship design and gunnery (longer-range guns and faster ‘race-built’ galleons designed by Hawkins), the failure of the ‘join with Parma’ plan, English fireships at Calais on the night of 7–8 August 1588, and the storms that scattered the fleet around Scotland and Ireland in September.

Spanish Invasion Plans

Philip II’s plan rested on a difficult piece of geography. The Armada would sail from Lisbon up the Channel to Calais. There it would meet the Duke of Parma’s 30,000 veteran troops in the Spanish Netherlands, escort them across the Channel in unprotected barges, and land in Kent. Once Parma’s army was on English soil, Catholic English subjects would (Philip hoped) rise up. The fleet was therefore not just a war fleet but a transport bodyguard.

Two structural problems hurt the plan from the start. First, the ‘original’ commander Santa Cruz — an experienced admiral — died in February 1588. Philip replaced him with the Duke of Medina Sidonia, a senior nobleman who frankly admitted in writing that he had no naval experience. Second, the rendezvous with Parma assumed perfect timing: the Armada had to arrive off Calais exactly when Parma’s barges were ready. There was no deep-water port on the Flemish coast where the great Spanish galleons could shelter while they waited.

The English Fleet

The Lord High Admiral, Lord Howard of Effingham, commanded around 200 English ships from Plymouth. Drake was vice-admiral; Hawkins and Frobisher led other squadrons. Sir John Hawkins had spent the 1570s and 1580s redesigning English warships into race-built galleons — lower hulls, no high ‘castles’ at bow and stern, and a long line of long-range guns down each side. The Spanish fleet, by contrast, was designed to grapple-and-board: bigger, taller, packed with soldiers, but slower and with shorter-range cannon mounted differently.

The English knew they could not stop the Armada by ramming or boarding. Their plan was to use longer-range gunfire to keep the fight at a distance, harass the formation, and use the wind to attack from the rear — never letting Spain force a close-quarters fight on Spanish terms.

The Channel Battles, 31 July – 6 August

The Armada was first sighted off the Lizard on 19 July. From 31 July to 6 August the two fleets fought a running battle up the English Channel: skirmishes off Plymouth (31 July), Portland Bill (2 August) and the Isle of Wight (3–4 August). The Spanish kept their disciplined crescent formation; the English snapped at the wings, picked off a few stragglers (most notably the Rosario, captured by Drake), but never broke the Spanish line. By 6 August the Armada was anchored off Calais, waiting for word from Parma.

The Fireships at Calais, Night of 7–8 August

Parma’s news was bad: his barges were not ready, and the Dutch ‘Sea Beggars’ were blockading the inshore waters around Dunkirk. The Armada could not approach to take Parma’s troops on board; Parma could not come out. Lord Howard chose his moment. On the night of 7–8 August he sent eight unmanned fireships, packed with pitch and gunpowder and set on fire, drifting on the tide into the anchored Spanish fleet.

The fireships caused little physical damage — the Spanish cut their anchor cables and scattered — but the loss of formation was disastrous. Anchors were left on the seabed off Calais. The crescent never reformed.

The Battle of Gravelines, 8 August

The next day the English caught the broken Armada off Gravelines and fought the only sustained pitched battle of the campaign. Closing to within musket range, the English used their long-range guns to hammer the Spanish hulls for eight hours. Three Spanish galleons were sunk or driven aground; many others were badly damaged. The Spanish formation was wrecked, and the wind swung to the south-west, pushing the Armada into the North Sea, away from Parma, and away from any chance of return.

The Long Way Home

Medina Sidonia took the only route left: north around Scotland and west of Ireland to reach Spain. In September violent Atlantic storms scattered the fleet. The unseasoned water casks — a direct legacy of Drake’s 1587 raid on Cadiz — leaked, leaving crews dehydrated. Around two dozen ships were wrecked on the Scottish and Irish coasts; thousands of sailors and soldiers drowned or were killed by Crown soldiers when they crawled ashore. Of 130 ships that left Lisbon, fewer than 70 made it home, and most of those were unfit for further service.

Key Fact

On the night of 7–8 August 1588, Lord Howard sent eight English fireships into the anchored Spanish fleet at Calais. The fireships destroyed almost nothing but broke the Armada’s formation, prevented the planned link-up with Parma, and exposed the fleet to the English broadsides at Gravelines the next day.

Why the English Won — Weighing the Factors

A weak answer says ‘the weather beat the Armada’. Storms certainly destroyed the fleet on the way home, but by then the campaign was already lost — the storms killed a defeated Armada, not a winning one. The deeper causes interconnect.

Edexcel examiners specifically flag ‘the weather beat the Armada’ as a single-factor answer that caps below the top band. The storms hit AFTER the campaign was already decided. By 9 August the Armada had lost its formation at Calais, been mauled at Gravelines, missed Parma, and been blown into the North Sea. Top-band answers explain that the storms were the killing blow on a fleet that English ship design, English fireships, Spanish supply failures and the broken Parma plan had already defeated. Storms are part of the answer, not the answer.

English advantages came from preparation. Hawkins’s race-built galleons gave the fleet superior speed and gunnery. Drake’s Cadiz raid the previous April had destroyed the seasoned timber for water casks, leaving the Armada with leaking supplies. Lord Howard chose his moments well — the fireships at Calais were the single most important tactical decision of the campaign. Spanish problems were structural: Medina Sidonia’s inexperience, the missing deep-water port for the Parma rendezvous, the impossible coordination required between Lisbon and the Netherlands, and the Dutch Sea Beggars blockading the Flemish coast. The storms then finished the work the campaign had already begun.

For 16-mark judgement questions, examiners reward weighing factors and reaching a defended overall view. A simple structure: short-term tactical reason (fireships and Gravelines), structural English advantages (Hawkins’s race-built ships and gunnery), Spanish failures (Medina Sidonia, no port, Parma plan), then the storms as finishing factor. Conclude on which mattered most and why — many strong answers argue the fireships were the decisive moment because they broke the formation that everything else depended on.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Philip II’s plan was to sail the Armada (130 ships, 24,000 men under Medina Sidonia) up the Channel to escort the Duke of Parma’s 30,000 troops from the Netherlands to invade Kent.
  • The plan broke at Calais on the night of 7–8 August 1588 when English fireships scattered the Armada’s formation, preventing the link-up with Parma; the next day Lord Howard’s fleet hammered the broken formation at Gravelines.
  • English victory was multi-factor — Hawkins’s race-built galleons and gunnery, Drake’s 1587 Cadiz raid destroying water-cask timber, leadership, the failure of the Parma rendezvous, and finally the storms that wrecked the retreating fleet around Scotland and Ireland.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the English fleet that fought the Spanish Armada in 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Race-built galleons designed by John Hawkins — lower hulls, no high ‘castles’ at bow and stern, faster and more manoeuvrable than older galleons.
• Long-range gunnery — English guns could fire broadsides at greater distance, allowing the fleet to attack the Armada without grappling and boarding on Spanish terms.
• Experienced commanders under Lord Howard of Effingham — with Drake as vice-admiral and Hawkins and Frobisher leading squadrons.
• Use of fireships — eight unmanned ships filled with pitch and gunpowder were set adrift into the Spanish fleet at Calais on the night of 7–8 August 1588.

Mastering: Two clearly developed features with precise supporting detail.
Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
Emerging: One simple feature identified.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the fireships at Calais were so important to the English victory.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• They broke the Spanish formation — the disciplined crescent had survived a week of running battles in the Channel; the fireships forced Spanish captains to cut anchors and scatter.
• They prevented the Parma rendezvous — with the fleet broken and pushed away from Calais, there was no longer a coherent force to escort Parma’s barges across the Channel.
• They exposed the Armada to Gravelines — the next day Lord Howard’s fleet caught the disordered Spanish ships at close range and hammered them with broadsides for eight hours.
• They cost the Spanish their anchors — ships that had cut cables off Calais were unable to anchor again on the storm-bound coasts of Scotland and Ireland on the way home.

Mastering: Two reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why the Spanish Armada failed in 1588.
You may use the following in your answer:
• English ship design
• the storms after the campaign
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links.

Indicative content:
• English ship design (stimulus) — Hawkins’s race-built galleons were faster, more manoeuvrable and carried longer-range guns, allowing English squadrons to attack from a safe distance and avoid the Spanish boarding tactics.
• Storms (stimulus) — September gales around Scotland and Ireland wrecked roughly two dozen ships and drowned thousands; the storms turned a defeat into a disaster.
• Fireships at Calais (own knowledge) — on the night of 7–8 August 1588, Lord Howard’s eight fireships broke the Spanish crescent formation, costing them their anchors and exposing them to Gravelines the next day.
• Failure of the Parma rendezvous (own knowledge) — there was no deep-water port for the Armada to wait in, the Dutch Sea Beggars were blockading the Flemish coast, and Parma’s barges were not ready.
• Spanish leadership and supply problems (own knowledge) — Medina Sidonia had no naval experience and admitted it in writing; Drake’s 1587 Cadiz raid had destroyed seasoned wood for water casks, so supplies leaked and spoiled at sea.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor. SPaG marks awarded separately for accurate spelling, punctuation and period-specific vocabulary (fireship, race-built, broadside, Privy Council, Armada, circumnavigation).

Arguments supporting the statement (fireships as decisive):
• The fireships broke the Spanish crescent formation at Calais on the night of 7–8 August 1588 — the formation that had survived every Channel battle.
• They prevented any link-up with Parma’s 30,000 troops, removing the entire purpose of the campaign.
• They cost the Spanish their anchors and exposed them to the Gravelines bombardment the following day.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• English ship design and gunnery (stimulus) — Hawkins’s race-built galleons and long-range broadsides made the running Channel battles winnable; without that, the fireships would have followed a coherent Spanish victory rather than a stalemate.
• Storms after Gravelines (stimulus) — September gales around Scotland and Ireland turned defeat into catastrophe, but they hit a fleet already broken; arguably they magnified the result rather than caused it.
• Failure of the Parma rendezvous (own knowledge) — the absence of a deep-water Flemish port and the Dutch Sea Beggars’ blockade meant the rendezvous would have failed even without the fireships.
• Spanish supply and leadership failures (own knowledge) — Medina Sidonia’s inexperience and the leaking unseasoned casks (a legacy of Cadiz 1587) weakened the fleet across the whole campaign.

Justified judgement: The fireships were the tactical hinge — they turned a stalemate into a defeat. But they only succeeded because English race-built ships had kept the campaign alive long enough, because the Parma plan was already breaking down, and because Spanish supply was already failing. Strong answers argue the fireships were decisive because they exploited weaknesses the other factors had created — no single factor on its own would have been enough.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement, accurate SPaG with period vocabulary.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached. Mostly accurate SPaG.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing; SPaG accurate enough for meaning.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or judgement; SPaG affecting clarity.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Spanish invasion plan for 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• A combined naval and land operation — 130 ships and around 24,000 men under Medina Sidonia would sail from Lisbon up the Channel to Calais.
• A planned rendezvous with the Duke of Parma — 30,000 veteran Spanish troops in the Netherlands would be escorted across the Channel in barges to land in Kent.
• Reliance on a Catholic rising in England — once Parma’s army landed, Philip expected English Catholics to support the invasion.
• Tight coordination required — the Armada had to arrive off Calais exactly when Parma’s barges were ready, with no deep-water port available for the great galleons to wait in.

Secure: Two features identified, at least one developed.
Developing: Two features identified without development, or one developed feature.
