practice_questions.text: Explain why the Spanish failed to link up with the Duke of Parma in August 1588.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• Parma’s barges were not ready on time — the assumption that Parma could appear at Calais on demand turned out to be unrealistic given the logistics of moving 30,000 men.
• The Dutch ‘Sea Beggars’ blockaded the Flemish coast — small Dutch warships made it impossible for Parma’s shallow barges to leave Dunkirk safely.
• There was no deep-water port for the Armada to shelter in — Medina Sidonia’s great galleons could not enter the shallows where Parma’s barges sat, leaving the fleet exposed at Calais.
• English fireships at Calais broke the Armada’s formation — on the night of 7–8 August the Spanish fleet cut its anchors and scattered, ending any chance of a coordinated meeting.

Mastering: Two reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

before.content_html:
For most Elizabethans, formal education was a privilege determined by social rank, gender and where you lived. A nobleman’s son might be tutored at home in Latin, Greek and the courtly arts; a yeoman’s daughter might learn only enough reading to follow the Bible. Yet the second half of the sixteenth century saw a real expansion of schooling — over 130 new grammar schools were founded in Elizabeth’s reign. Beyond the classroom, the same decades produced bear-baiting pits, real tennis courts and the first purpose-built theatres in London. Education and leisure together reveal how rigidly Elizabethan society was stratified by class — and how much it was changing.

Key Fact

Elizabethan education was layered by class and gender. Most children learned at home; nobility hired private tutors; some boys attended petty schools (ages 5–7) for basic reading and writing; grammar schools (ages 7–14) taught Latin to fee-paying or scholarship boys; girls were rarely formally schooled beyond reading.

Education in the Home

For nobility and gentry, the home was the main classroom. Boys destined for politics or the Church were taught Latin, Greek, French, dancing, riding and music by live-in tutors. Girls of the same rank learned reading, writing, music and needlework, alongside how to manage a large household. Elizabeth herself had been tutored at home by Roger Ascham — a humanist who later wrote that her Greek was better than most clergymen’s.

For the lower orders, ‘education’ meant practical training. A yeoman farmer’s child learned to plough, sew or brew alongside parents. From the age of about seven, many poorer boys entered an apprenticeship with a master craftsman, lasting around seven years. Girls usually went into domestic service. The Bible — in English after the 1559 Settlement — was often the only book a household owned, and parents who could read used it to teach the alphabet.

Petty Schools and Grammar Schools

A small minority of children attended petty schools from around age five. These were run from a parish room or a teacher’s home, often by a clergyman’s wife, and taught reading, writing and a little arithmetic using a hornbook — a wooden paddle showing the alphabet under a thin layer of horn. The Lord’s Prayer and Ten Commandments were standard texts, doubling as religious instruction.

From age seven, the academically able sons of the gentry, merchants and prosperous yeomen could move on to a grammar school. The day ran from 6am to 5pm in summer, with two short breaks. Pupils studied Latin grammar, classical literature (Cicero, Virgil, Ovid), rhetoric, and some Greek. Discipline was harsh: birching for poor work was routine. Fees varied — a few free places existed for poor boys with academic promise — but most pupils were the sons of those who could afford them. A handful of the brightest could go on to the universities of Oxford or Cambridge from around age fourteen.

Students sometimes assume that because grammar schools spread, most Elizabethans could read. They could not. By 1588 perhaps 30 per cent of men and far fewer women could sign their own name — and that was the rough test for basic literacy. Schooling was concentrated on noble and gentry boys, and London literacy ran higher than in rural Yorkshire or Cornwall. The expansion of schools matters because it widened access, not because it produced a reading public.

Sport and Pastimes

Leisure was as stratified as education. The wealthy hunted deer with hounds, hawked, played real tennis on enclosed courts, fenced and bowled on smooth lawns. Elizabeth was a keen rider and dancer, and the court’s entertainments shaped national fashion. Working people had less time and rougher pleasures. Football was played between villages with whole parishes as teams — effectively a brawl with a leather ball — and was repeatedly banned by local authorities for the injuries it caused.

The most popular spectator sports were violent. Bear-baiting drew crowds in Southwark, where chained bears fought packs of mastiffs while spectators wagered on the outcome. Cock-fighting, dog-fighting and bull-baiting were similar. The poor played skittles, dice and cards in alehouses; the gentry played chess and a fast-paced gambling card game called Primero. Dancing — from sedate court pavanes to leaping country galliards — crossed every social rank.

Key Fact

Elizabethan leisure split sharply by class. Hunting, hawking, real tennis, fencing and bowls were upper-class pursuits; football, bear-baiting, cock-fighting, skittles and alehouse cards were popular pastimes. Music and dancing were shared. The first purpose-built theatres in London opened from 1576, drawing audiences from every rank.

The Theatre

Before Elizabeth’s reign, plays were performed by travelling companies in inn yards or great halls. In 1576 James Burbage built the first permanent playhouse in London — called simply The Theatre — just outside the city walls in Shoreditch, beyond the reach of the Puritan-leaning London corporation. The Curtain followed in 1577 and Philip Henslowe’s Rose opened in 1587 on Bankside. Companies needed a noble patron to perform legally: the Lord Chamberlain’s Men and the Lord Admiral’s Men were the leading troupes by 1588.

A penny got you into the standing yard with the ‘groundlings’; another penny bought a seat in the galleries; a third let you sit on the stage itself. Audiences mixed apprentices with merchants and the occasional nobleman. Plays mixed bawdy comedy, history and tragedy — Christopher Marlowe’s Tamburlaine filled houses from 1587, and a young Shakespeare arrived in London at the end of the decade.

Puritans loathed the playhouses. They argued that crowds spread plague, that boys playing women’s parts encouraged immorality, that pickpockets and prostitutes worked the audiences, and that plays distracted apprentices from their work. The City of London authorities tried repeatedly to close the theatres, which is why Burbage built outside the city walls in the first place. Elizabeth herself enjoyed plays at court, and her favour — through the licensing system — kept the theatres open against Puritan pressure. The very feature that made the theatre suspect (mixing classes in one space) is what makes it useful evidence of a more shared popular culture by 1588.

Education and leisure together show two truths about Elizabethan society. First, class and gender governed almost everything — what you read, what you played, where you sat in the theatre. Second, the boundaries were starting to bend. More boys reached grammar schools than ever before, and the new playhouses brought apprentices and gentry into the same building, even if they paid different prices. By the time the Armada threatened in 1588, the cultural life of Elizabethan England was wider, noisier and more confident than the cautious country Elizabeth had inherited in 1558.
before.exam_tip_html: For 4-mark ‘Describe two features’ questions, give two clearly distinct features — for example, the curriculum of grammar schools and their daily routine count as one feature, not two. Develop each with a precise detail (the 6am start, the use of birching, Latin authors named). For 12-mark ‘Explain why’ questions on the rise of leisure or schooling, link causes — the Royal Injunctions of 1559 making the English Bible accessible, urban wealth funding new grammar schools, noble patronage shielding the playhouses from Puritan opposition. Use period vocabulary: petty school, hornbook, apprenticeship, groundlings, patron.

practice_questions.text: Explain why education expanded in Elizabethan England.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• The Royal Injunctions of 1559 required clergy to encourage Bible reading in English — this made basic literacy a religious duty for Protestant households and pushed parents to teach reading at home or send children to petty schools.
• Wealth from trade and farming created a ‘middling sort’ — merchants, prosperous yeomen and gentry could afford grammar school fees and saw schooling as the route into law, the Church and government service.
• Charitable foundation by guilds, towns and individuals — over 130 new grammar schools were founded under Elizabeth, often endowed in wills as a form of public-spirited philanthropy.
• Government concern with social order — an educated, Protestant elite was seen as a defence against Catholicism and rebellion; the same logic that funded universities funded grammar schools.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why theatre became popular in Elizabethan England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• noble patronage
• purpose-built playhouses
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links. Indicative content: • Noble patronage (stimulus) — companies such as the Lord Chamberlain’s Men and the Lord Admiral’s Men needed an aristocratic patron to perform legally; without it they could be punished as vagabonds under the 1572 Act. Patronage protected actors and gave their plays prestige. • Purpose-built playhouses (stimulus) — from 1576 (The Theatre), 1577 (The Curtain) and 1587 (The Rose), London had permanent venues capable of holding 2,000–3,000 spectators, replacing temporary inn-yard performances and creating a daily entertainment industry. • Tiered ticket pricing (own knowledge) — a penny got entry to the yard, two pence a gallery seat; this allowed apprentices, merchants and gentry to attend the same play, making theatre genuinely popular across classes. • Royal favour (own knowledge) — Elizabeth enjoyed plays at court and her licensing system shielded the theatres from the Puritan-leaning London corporation that wanted them closed. • Talented playwrights (own knowledge) — Christopher Marlowe’s Tamburlaine from 1587 brought blank verse and large historical themes to mass audiences, raising the artistic standing of theatre. Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge. Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone. practice_questions.text: Explain why leisure activities differed between rich and poor Elizabethans.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• Cost and access — hunting required deer parks, hawks, horses and trained falconers; real tennis required enclosed courts found only in noble houses or palaces; these pursuits were physically out of reach for the poor.
• Time available — labourers, apprentices and farm workers had limited free hours and most leisure happened on Sundays after church, leading to alehouse games (skittles, dice, cards) and parish football rather than long ritualised pursuits.
• Class identity and display — nobility and gentry used hawking, hunting and dancing the pavane to display refinement; gambling at chess and Primero showed wealth they could afford to lose. Leisure was a way of performing rank.
• Shared violent spectatorship — bear-baiting and cock-fighting drew all classes because they were cheap to attend and depended on betting; this is one area where rich and poor mingled despite the wider divide.

Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (Protestantism as main reason):
• Royal Injunctions of 1559 (stimulus) required clergy to promote Bible reading in English, making literacy a Protestant duty and pushing parents toward formal schooling for their sons.
• Grammar school curriculum reinforced Protestant worship — pupils learned to read the Prayer Book, the Bible and the Ten Commandments alongside Latin classics.
• Many new schools were founded with explicitly Protestant aims by Anglican clergy, town corporations and reform-minded merchants.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• The growing ‘middling sort’ (stimulus) — merchants and prosperous yeomen could now afford grammar school fees and saw schooling as a ladder into law, the Church and government, fuelling demand regardless of religion.
• Charitable philanthropy (own knowledge) — guilds, livery companies and individuals endowed schools in their wills as public-spirited acts; this was a long Tudor tradition pre-dating Protestantism.
• Government concern with social order (own knowledge) — an educated Protestant elite was seen as a defence against Catholic recusancy and foreign threat, so political insecurity (especially after 1570 excommunication) drove foundations as much as religious zeal.
• Continuity from earlier reigns (own knowledge) — grammar schools had been founded throughout the Tudor period; the Elizabethan expansion accelerated an existing pattern rather than starting it.

Justified judgement: Protestantism gave moral and political weight to schooling and the Royal Injunctions made literacy a religious duty, but the practical drivers were the wealth and aspirations of the ‘middling sort’ and a charitable foundation tradition that pre-dated the Reformation. A strong response weighs religious motivation against social and economic causes and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

before.content_html:
Behind the courtly image of an Elizabethan ‘Golden Age’ sat a sharp social crisis. The numbers on the move — tramping the roads in search of work, food or shelter — rose dramatically between 1558 and 1588. Contemporaries called these wandering poor vagabonds, and they frightened the propertied classes far more than they ever frightened the queen. The story of how Elizabeth’s government responded — from whippings in 1572 to compulsory rates for the poor by 1601 — is the story of attitudes hardening, then thawing, into the first national system of poor relief in English history.

Key Fact

Elizabethan poverty rose because of population growth (from c.3 million in 1558 to c.4 million by 1600), rising prices, sheep enclosures replacing arable farming, the dissolution of the monasteries (which had given charity), bad harvests in the 1580s, and the demobilisation of soldiers from foreign wars. Elizabethans split the poor into the ‘impotent’ (deserving) and the ‘sturdy beggars’ or vagabonds (undeserving).

Why Was Poverty Rising?

Several pressures combined. England’s population grew by roughly a third in the second half of the sixteenth century — without a matching growth in food production. Demand pushed prices up; price inflation hit wage labourers hardest because their pay rose much more slowly than the cost of bread. Contemporaries blamed wickedness or laziness; modern historians point to demographic and economic causes.

Land use shifted. Wool prices made sheep more profitable than crops, so landowners enclosed common fields with hedges and ditches. Enclosure displaced labourers who had relied on common land for grazing and gleaning, and one shepherd could now manage land that had previously employed a dozen ploughmen. After Henry VIII’s dissolution of the monasteries in the 1530s, the network of monastic almshouses, hospitals and direct charity that had cushioned medieval poverty was largely gone — the gap had still not been filled by Elizabeth’s reign. Bad harvests in 1586 and 1587 pushed already-fragile households over the edge, and demobilised soldiers returning from the Netherlands and Ireland added to the wandering population.

The Deserving and the Undeserving

Tudor authorities did not see ‘the poor’ as one group. They drew a sharp moral line. The impotent poor — the old, the sick, orphaned children, those with disabilities — were seen as deserving help. The able-bodied poor who refused work were sturdy beggars or vagabonds — suspected of being criminal, idle and dangerous. The line between ‘cannot work’ and ‘will not work’ was not always honest, but it shaped every policy that followed.

Students sometimes absorb a ‘Golden Age’ image of Elizabeth’s reign — The Theatre, Drake, fashion, Gloriana — and skip the same decades’ sharp rise in poverty. Both are true at the same time. Drake circumnavigated the globe in 1577–80 while the 1572 Vagabonds Act ordered first-offence vagabonds to be whipped and burned through the ear. The Edexcel spec deliberately puts poverty alongside exploration and Virginia in Key topic 3 to make this judgement testable. Top-band answers acknowledge both, rather than picking one image and writing about it alone.

Attitudes Hardening: The 1572 Vagabonds Act

Early Elizabethan policy was punitive. The 1547 Vagrancy Act under Edward VI had even allowed vagabonds to be branded and enslaved — that was repealed, but the instinct to terrify wanderers off the roads survived. Elizabeth’s 1572 Vagabonds Act ordered that any able-bodied person caught wandering without work could be whipped and bored through the right ear with a hot iron for a first offence. A second offence could mean execution. Travelling actors needed a noble patron, otherwise they too could be treated as vagabonds — the same Act that protected Burbage’s playhouse companies threatened those without a master.

The 1572 Act made one important new decision: it required Justices of the Peace in every parish to keep a register of the ‘impotent poor’ and to set a compulsory poor rate — a local tax — to support them. For the first time, helping the deserving poor was not optional charity but a legal duty on every parish.

Attitudes Softening: The 1576 Poor Relief Act

Within four years the tone shifted. The 1576 Poor Relief Act made parishes provide raw materials — wool, flax, hemp, iron — on which the able-bodied poor could be set to work. Those who refused work were sent to a House of Correction (also called a Bridewell, after the prototype in London) for hard labour. The change was small but significant: the law now recognised that some people genuinely wanted to work but could not find it. Punishment remained, but provision for honest labour appeared alongside it.

A few currents pushed in the same direction. Towns such as Norwich and Ipswich had already pioneered local schemes that distinguished the genuinely unemployed from the wilfully idle — Norwich’s 1570 census of the poor identified deserving recipients ward by ward. Protestant clergy preached that the poor were Christ’s neighbours, not just a public-order problem. And the simple visibility of unemployed but able-bodied men — demobilised soldiers, displaced labourers — made it harder to dismiss everyone on the road as a wilful vagabond. By the late 1580s, JPs were registering the impotent poor, levying rates, and putting the able-bodied to work in their own parishes rather than driving them away.

Where Things Stood by 1588

By the year of the Armada, the framework of an early national system was in place. Each parish kept its own poor on its own books. Vagabonds caught moving between parishes were still whipped and returned to their place of birth. The deserving impotent received pensions, food and small payments funded by the compulsory poor rate. The able-bodied were given materials and put to work, with the House of Correction as the threat for those who refused. The fully developed Poor Laws of 1597 and 1601 — the famous Elizabethan Poor Law — built directly on these foundations laid between 1572 and 1576.

Key Fact

The 1572 Vagabonds Act introduced harsh punishments (whipping, burning through the ear) but also required JPs to keep a register of the impotent poor and levy a compulsory poor rate. The 1576 Poor Relief Act required parishes to provide work materials for the able-bodied, with Houses of Correction for those who refused. Together they laid the foundations for the 1601 Elizabethan Poor Law.

Two changes ran beneath the legislation. The first was a slow recognition that poverty had causes — harvest failure, demobilisation, enclosure, inflation — that were beyond an individual’s control. The second was the principle that the parish, funded by compulsory taxation of its better-off inhabitants, carried legal responsibility for its own poor. Neither idea was fully accepted in 1588, and both would harden into law only after Elizabeth’s reign — but both were in place before the Armada sailed.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the 1572 Vagabonds Act.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per feature (1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail). Maximum 4 marks.

Indicative content:
• Harsh punishment of able-bodied wanderers — first-offence vagabonds were to be whipped and bored through the right ear with a hot iron; a second offence could mean execution.
• Compulsory parish responsibility for the impotent poor — Justices of the Peace in every parish were required to keep a register of the deserving poor and levy a compulsory poor rate to support them.
• Restrictions on travelling performers — actors and minstrels without a noble patron could be treated as vagabonds, which is why companies needed patronage from figures like the Lord Chamberlain.
• Use of Justices of the Peace as enforcers — JPs were given the legal authority to identify, register, punish and relieve the poor of their parish, professionalising local enforcement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain why poverty increased in Elizabethan England.
You may use the following in your answer:
• population growth
• enclosure
You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by precise detail. Top band requires at least three reasons (using both stimulus points AND own knowledge) with clear causal links.

Indicative content:
• Population growth (stimulus) — England’s population rose from roughly 3 million in 1558 toward 4 million by 1600. Demand for food outstripped supply, pushing up prices and squeezing wage labourers whose wages did not keep pace.
• Enclosure (stimulus) — landowners hedged off arable common land for sheep because wool was profitable; one shepherd replaced many ploughmen, displacing rural labourers from their employment and from common rights.
• Price inflation (own knowledge) — food and goods prices rose sharply across the sixteenth century while wages lagged, pushing wage-earning households below subsistence even when in work.
• Dissolution of the monasteries (own knowledge) — Henry VIII’s 1530s dissolution had ended the monastic almshouses, hospitals and daily charity that had cushioned medieval poverty; the gap had still not been filled by Elizabeth’s reign.
• Bad harvests of 1586 and 1587 (own knowledge) — back-to-back failed harvests pushed fragile households into vagabondage; demobilised soldiers returning from the Netherlands and Ireland added to the wandering population.

Mastering: At least three reasons fully explained, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, with clear interconnections.
Secure: Three reasons explained with mostly accurate detail; uses stimulus and own knowledge.
Developing: Two reasons explained, may rely heavily on stimulus alone.
Emerging: One reason or simple description without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Elizabeth’s government changed its policies towards the poor between 1572 and 1576.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• Recognition that poverty had economic causes — demobilised soldiers and labourers displaced by enclosure made it visible that many able-bodied poor wanted work but could not find it, pushing the 1576 Act to provide raw materials for parish work.
• Influence of pioneering town schemes — Norwich’s 1570 census of the poor and Ipswich’s relief schemes had shown that distinguishing the genuinely unemployed from the wilfully idle worked better than punishment alone.
• Protestant religious thinking — clergy increasingly preached that the poor were Christ’s neighbours and a moral duty, not simply a public-order problem.
• Concern about social order — the Privy Council feared that mass vagabondage could lead to rebellion; constructive provision of work in the parish, backed up by Houses of Correction for those who refused, was seen as more effective than the 1572 punishments alone.

Mastering: Two reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

practice_questions.type: 16 marks — Make and Defend a Judgement
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for a sustained argument that uses both stimulus points AND at least one factor of own knowledge, weighs them against each other, and reaches a substantiated overall judgement on the named factor.

Arguments supporting the statement (failure of harsh punishment as main reason):
• 1572 Vagabonds Act (stimulus) — whipping and burning through the ear did not stop people from moving in search of work; numbers of vagabonds remained high, showing punishment alone was not deterring those driven by genuine need.
• Visibility of demobilised soldiers and displaced labourers undermined the assumption that all wanderers were wilfully idle, forcing a rethink of the 1572 approach.
• The 1576 Poor Relief Act explicitly added work materials and Houses of Correction, recognising that punishment without provision of work was insufficient.

Arguments against (other factors more important):
• Norwich’s 1570 census of the poor (stimulus) — town schemes had already begun distinguishing impotent from sturdy poor before national punishment had clearly ‘failed’; pioneering local practice drove change as much as national failure did.
• Protestant religious thinking (own knowledge) — clergy preached the poor as a Christian duty, shaping attitudes among landowners and JPs and making compulsory poor rates politically possible.
• Economic reality of population growth, inflation and bad harvests (own knowledge) — the scale of the crisis (especially after 1586) made parish-level provision a practical necessity regardless of attitudes.
• Concern with social order (own knowledge) — the Privy Council saw constructive provision of work as a defence against rebellion, not just charity; political calculation drove change as much as moral failure of punishment.

Justified judgement: The harshness of 1572 did fail in its own terms — vagabondage continued — and that failure pushed the move toward provision of work in 1576. But the change of attitude rested equally on town pioneers like Norwich, on Protestant teaching, and on the sheer economic scale of the crisis. A strong response weighs the failure of punishment against these other drivers and reaches a defended overall view.

Mastering: Sustained argument weighing all factors, both stimulus points used AND own knowledge added, substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with most factors weighed; judgement reached but less developed.
Developing: Some argument and limited weighing of factors.
Emerging: Description of factors without weighing or clear judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain why Elizabethan authorities distinguished between the ‘impotent poor’ and the ‘sturdy beggars’.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for explained reasons supported by accurate detail. Highest band requires at least two explained reasons with sustained focus on causation.

Indicative content (any two reasons developed):
• Religious and moral framework — Tudor Christianity taught that helping the genuinely needy was a duty but encouraging the lazy was sinful; the distinction allowed authorities to be generous to the deserving while punishing the ‘wilfully idle’.
• Public order concerns — able-bodied wanderers were feared as potential criminals and rebels (especially after the 1569 Northern Rebellion), so framing them as ‘sturdy beggars’ justified harsh deterrent punishments under the 1572 Act.
• Cost control — if every poor person counted equally, the parish poor rate would be unaffordable; restricting compulsory relief to the impotent kept the cost on the rate-payers manageable.
• Limits of medieval understanding — contemporaries lacked modern economic explanations and assumed that anyone who could work would find work; the moral binary made sense within that worldview, even though it disguised structural causes such as inflation, enclosure and bad harvests.

Mastering: Two reasons fully explained with precise detail and clear causal links.
Secure: Two reasons explained with mostly accurate detail.
Developing: One reason explained, or two reasons identified without explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification without explanation.

lessons.title: Exploration, Drake's circumnavigation and the Virginia colony

before.content_html:
By 1577 a small Plymouth ship called the Pelican slipped out of Plymouth Sound carrying Francis Drake, a crew of 164 and a secret commission from Elizabeth herself. Three years later Drake returned to Plymouth in his renamed flagship Golden Hind, having sailed around the entire world — only the second captain in history to do so. While Drake counted his Spanish silver, a separate set of voyages was probing the coast of North America, and by 1585 Sir Walter Raleigh had landed the first English settlers on Roanoke Island in modern-day North Carolina. Drake’s circumnavigation and the failed Virginia colony are two halves of the same Elizabethan ambition — reach further, trade more, beat Spain — but they ended very differently.

Key Fact

Elizabethan exploration was driven by the desire to expand trade beyond cloth markets in northern Europe, the chance to attack Spanish shipping for gold and silver, the search for a north-west passage to Asia, and the patriotic and religious wish to challenge Catholic Spain. New ship designs (galleons), better navigation tools (astrolabe, quadrant, more accurate maps) and the printed sailing directions of Richard Hakluyt made longer voyages possible.

Why Did Elizabethans Sail Further?

English trade in 1558 was overwhelmingly with Antwerp — raw wool and finished cloth across the narrow seas. When religious wars in the Netherlands disrupted the Antwerp market in the 1560s, English merchants needed new outlets. Joint-stock trading companies were chartered to push into the Baltic, the Mediterranean, Russia and West Africa.

Three other motives mattered. First, Spain’s American empire flooded Europe with silver bullion every year — Elizabethan privateers wanted a share. Second, men like Sir Humphrey Gilbert and John Davis searched for a north-west passage through the Arctic to the riches of Asia, hoping to bypass Spanish and Portuguese routes. Third, the geographer Richard Hakluyt argued in his 1582 Divers Voyages Touching the Discoverie of America that England needed colonies for trade, prestige and as bases against Spain. Patriotic, Protestant and commercial arguments reinforced one another.

Ships, Maps and Sailors

The technology made it possible. The English galleon — refined under naval administrator Sir John Hawkins — had a longer, lower hull than the older Spanish carrack. It carried more cannon along its sides and could turn faster, ideal for the running gun battles that suited English captains. Astrolabes and quadrants let navigators measure latitude from the sun and the pole star; new printed charts (notably Mercator’s 1569 projection) made plotting long ocean courses easier. Logbooks recording wind patterns built up reliable knowledge of the Atlantic. By the 1580s an English captain could plan a voyage to West Africa, the Caribbean or even round Cape Horn with a confidence unimaginable a generation earlier.

It is tempting to see Drake as a swashbuckling hero, knighted on his own deck. The same generation, however, included Sir John Hawkins, who from the 1560s ran Crown-backed voyages to West Africa where he attacked Portuguese ships and trafficked enslaved Africans across the Atlantic to sell to Spanish colonists in the Caribbean — voyages on which Drake sailed as a young man. The Edexcel spec foregrounds Drake’s circumnavigation, not Hawkins’s slaving raids, but a top-band answer is aware that English ‘exploration’ included violence and the trade in enslaved people, not only navigation. The Pearson 2026 terminology guidance asks us to write ‘enslaved person’, not ‘slave’.

Drake’s Circumnavigation, 1577–80

In December 1577 Drake left Plymouth with five ships, officially bound for the Mediterranean. The real plan, agreed in secret with Elizabeth, was to sail through the Strait of Magellan and raid Spanish silver shipping along the unprotected Pacific coast of South America. Of the original five ships, only the renamed Golden Hind reached the Pacific. Drake captured the Spanish treasure ship Nuestra Señora de la Concepción — nicknamed by sailors the Cacafuego — off the coast of Peru in March 1579, taking 26 tons of silver, 80 pounds of gold and chests of jewels. Rather than return through the Magellan Strait where the Spanish would be waiting, he sailed up the Pacific coast as far as modern-day California, claimed it for Elizabeth, and then crossed the Pacific to the Spice Islands and home around the Cape of Good Hope.

He reached Plymouth on 26 September 1580. The voyage’s plunder paid every investor a return of about £47 for every £1 invested — including Elizabeth, secretly the largest backer. The queen knighted Drake on the deck of the Golden Hind at Deptford in April 1581, an act of public defiance towards Philip II that horrified the Spanish ambassador.

Why Was the Circumnavigation Significant?

The voyage mattered for several reasons. Politically, it was a deliberate humiliation of Spain and the most provocative act of Elizabethan privateering yet. Economically, the bullion strengthened the Crown’s finances and turned circumnavigation from theory into a profitable speculation. Strategically, Drake had charted Pacific coasts the Spanish had assumed were closed to outsiders and proved that English ships and seamanship could match Spain’s. Personally, it confirmed Drake’s status as a national hero and Elizabeth’s most trusted privateer — the man she would send to ‘singe the King of Spain’s beard’ at Cadiz in 1587 and command against the Armada in 1588.

Key Fact

Drake left Plymouth in December 1577 and returned on 26 September 1580 in the Golden Hind, having captured the Spanish treasure ship Cacafuego off Peru. Investors received about £47 for every £1 invested. Elizabeth knighted Drake on the deck of the Golden Hind at Deptford in April 1581 — a deliberate insult to Philip II.

Raleigh and the Attempted Colonisation of Virginia

In 1584 Elizabeth granted Sir Walter Raleigh a six-year charter to colonise unclaimed land in North America. Raleigh, a court favourite, never sailed himself but financed the expeditions and named the new region Virginia in honour of the ‘Virgin Queen’. A scouting voyage in 1584 reached the Outer Banks of present-day North Carolina, where the captains met the Algonquian-speaking Indigenous peoples of Roanoke Island and brought back two men, Manteo and Wanchese, to London.

In April 1585 Raleigh dispatched Sir Richard Grenville with about 600 colonists and supply ships. They landed on Roanoke Island in August. The first settlement was led by Ralph Lane, a soldier rather than a farmer, and consisted largely of soldiers and gentlemen rather than experienced cultivators or craftsmen. By summer 1586 they were starving, on poor terms with Wingina’s Roanoke people, and a passing English fleet under Drake (returning from raids in the Caribbean) took them home.

Why Did the First Settlement Fail?

Several causes combined. The colonists were unsuited to the work — soldiers and gentlemen, not farmers; food ran out within months. Relations with the Indigenous Roanoke people, fragile from the start, broke down after Lane killed Wingina in 1586, ending any hope of trade for food. Roanoke Island itself had a poor harbour for resupply ships. The promised relief fleet from England was diverted to fight the Spanish in the Caribbean. And by 1587, Raleigh’s second attempt — led by John White and including women and children — arrived to find the first colony abandoned. White returned to England for supplies, was delayed by the Armada in 1588, and when he finally got back in 1590 the second settlement had vanished, leaving only the carved word CROATOAN. The fate of the ‘Lost Colony’ remains unknown.

The 16-mark essay reward is for weighing several causes — not for picking one. Top-band answers connect the failure of the first settlement (1585–86) and the disappearance of the second (1587–90) into a chain. The poor choice of colonists and a chosen leader (Lane) suited to soldiering rather than farming created food shortages; the killing of Wingina destroyed Indigenous co-operation; the Armada in 1588 prevented relief reaching the second colony just as it most needed it. Add Spain — the wider war pulled English shipping away from Roanoke at the critical moment — and you have a multi-cause judgement that an examiner can reward.

By 1588 Drake’s circumnavigation had given Elizabethan England a confident maritime self-image; Raleigh’s Roanoke had shown that ambition was not enough on its own. Both stories belong on the same page: an Age of Exploration that expanded trade and prestige, but did so unevenly, violently, and at a cost that the ‘Golden Age’ label hides.
before.exam_tip_html: For 12-mark causation on Elizabethan exploration, link multiple drivers — the loss of the Antwerp cloth market, Spanish silver as a target, the search for the north-west passage, and Hakluyt’s arguments for colonies. For 16-mark judgements on Drake’s significance or the failure of Virginia, weigh several factors and reach a substantiated overall view: was the failure of Roanoke about colonist choice, Indigenous relations, supply lines, or the Armada? On these ‘with SPaG’ questions, accuracy and period vocabulary are rewarded — use galleon, privateer, circumnavigation, colony, charter, Indigenous peoples — not loose phrases.
